That winter was miserable. On some errand days Sara had to tramp through snow; worse were the days when it thawed into muddy slush. At other times the fog lay so thick that street lamps burned from morning to night. London looked just as it had on that afternoon years earlier, when Sara had ridden through its streets curled up in the cab beside her father's shoulder. In such weather the Large Family's windows seemed wonderfully welcoming and snug, and the Indian gentleman's study glowed with rich colours and warmth. The attic, by contrast, was dreary beyond description. There seemed to be no sunrises or sunsets any more, and hardly a star. Low clouds covered the skylight, grey or mud-brown, or pouring rain. Even without a particularly heavy fog, daylight had gone by four in the afternoon. Sara needed a candle whenever she had to fetch something from her room. The kitchen women were miserable, which sharpened their tempers still further. They worked Becky like a little slave.

One night Becky crept into the attic and told Sara hoarsely, "If it wasn't for you, miss—for you an' the Bastille an' me bein' the prisoner next door—I think I'd die. It's gettin' real, isn't it? Every day the missus is more like the head jailer. I can almost see those big keys you say she's got. Cook's one of the jailers under her. Please tell me more, miss. Tell me about the underground passage we've dug beneath the walls."

Shivering, Sara answered, "I'll give you a warmer story. Bring your coverlet and wrap yourself up. I'll use mine, and we'll sit close together on the bed. I'll tell you about the tropical forest where the Indian gentleman's monkey lived. When he's on the table by the window, gazing at the street with that sorrowful face, I'm always sure he's remembering the forest where he swung by his tail from coconut trees. I wonder who captured him. And did he leave a family who counted on him to bring them coconuts?"
"That does sound warmer, miss," Becky said gratefully. "Though somehow even the Bastille warms me up a bit when you're tellin' me about it."

"That's because it gives you something else to think about," Sara explained. She wrapped herself so thoroughly that only her little dark face peeped out. "I've noticed how it works. When your body is miserable, you have to set your mind to thinking of something different."
Looking at her admiringly, Becky asked with some hesitation, "Can you manage that, miss?"
For a moment Sara drew her brows together.

"Sometimes yes, sometimes no," she answered bravely. "But when I CAN, I feel all right. I think we could always manage it if we practised enough. Lately I've been practising a great deal, and it's getting easier. When everything's dreadful—perfectly dreadful—I concentrate as hard as I possibly can on being a princess. I tell myself, 'I am a princess, and I am a fairy one, and because I am a fairy nothing can hurt me or make me uncomfortable.'" She laughed. "You can't imagine how it helps you forget."

There was no shortage of chances to direct her thoughts elsewhere, or of tests to discover whether she truly was a princess. But among the hardest came one terrible day that she often thought afterwards would stay with her, never entirely fading from memory however many years passed.

Rain had fallen for days. The streets were cold and slushy, filled with dreary chilly mist; sticky London mud lay everywhere beneath a shroud of fog and drizzle. Naturally, there were many long, wearisome errands—there always were in weather like that. Again and again Sara was sent out, until the damp had worked right through her shabby clothes. The ridiculous old feathers in her pitiful hat drooped more absurdly than ever. Her worn-down shoes were so saturated that they could take in no more water. Miss Minchin had also decided to punish her by withholding dinner. Cold, hungry, and exhausted, she began to look pinched about the face. Occasionally a kind passer-by glanced at her with sudden pity, but Sara never noticed. She hurried along, struggling to occupy her mind with something else. The need was desperate. With all her remaining strength she tried to "pretend" and "suppose." Yet this time it was harder than it had ever been. Once or twice the effort seemed almost to increase her hunger and cold instead of easing them. Still, she persisted stubbornly. Muddy water squelched through her broken shoes, and the wind tugged as though trying to tear off her thin jacket. As she walked she held a silent conversation with herself, neither speaking aloud nor moving her lips.

"Suppose my clothes were dry," she imagined. "Suppose I had sound shoes, a thick long coat, merino stockings, and an umbrella without holes. And suppose—just suppose—that beside a bakery selling hot buns I found sixpence with no owner. SUPPOSE I did: I'd go straight inside and buy six buns, the very hottest, and eat every one without pausing."
Sometimes the world allows remarkably strange things to happen.

What happened to Sara was certainly strange. Just as those thoughts were passing through her mind, she needed to cross the road. The mud was so deep that crossing was almost wading. She chose each step carefully, though it did little to keep her clean. But watching her steps meant watching her feet and the muddy ground. As she reached the pavement, something glittered in the gutter. It truly was silver: a tiny coin, trampled by countless feet, with just enough spirit remaining to give a faint shine. Not sixpence, but almost the next best thing—a fourpenny piece.
An instant later she held it in her cold, red-and-blue little hand.
"Oh," she gasped, "it really happened! It's true!"

Then, believe it or not, she looked directly at the shop in front of her. It was a bakery. A cheerful, plump, motherly woman with rosy cheeks was setting a tray in the window: delicious buns newly drawn from the oven, hot, round, and glossy, studded with currants.
For a few seconds Sara almost fainted. The surprise, the sight of those buns, and the lovely smell of warm bread rising from the baker's cellar window were nearly too much.

She knew there was no reason not to spend the coin. It had plainly lain in the mud a while. Among the crowds that pushed and jostled past all day, its owner had vanished beyond any hope of finding them.

Still feeling faint, she told herself, "But first I'll ask the woman in the bakery whether she's lost anything." She crossed the pavement and set one wet foot on the doorstep. There, a sight made her stop.

A small figure sat there, even more wretched than Sara. It was scarcely more than a heap of rags, with little bare feet showing, red and muddy, because the girl kept trying to cover them and the rags were too short. Above the bundle rose a tangle of uncombed hair and a dirty face with great hollow eyes, full of hunger.
The instant Sara saw those eyes she recognized their hunger, and pity rose in her.
With a small sigh she thought, "Here is one of the populace, and she's even hungrier than I am."

The child, this "one of the populace," looked up at Sara and edged aside to let her through. Giving way to everyone was a familiar duty. She knew a policeman, if he happened to spot her, would simply order her to "move on."
Tightening her fingers around the fourpenny piece, Sara stood undecided for a moment. Then she addressed the girl.
"Do you feel hungry?" she asked.
The girl shifted herself and her bundle of rags again.
"Don't I just," she rasped. "You bet I am."
Sara asked, "Have you had nothing for dinner?"
"No dinner," came the still-hoarser answer, with another shuffle. "No breakfast neither. No supper. Nothin' at all."
Sara asked, "Since when?"
"Can't say. Had nothin' today, nowhere. Kept askin' and askin'."
The sight alone made Sara feel hungrier and fainter. Yet her strange little thoughts were working inside her head. Heartsick though she was, she went on speaking silently to herself.

"If I'm a princess—if I'm one—when princesses were poor and forced from their thrones, they always shared with the populace when they found someone poorer and hungrier than themselves. They always did. Each bun costs a penny. With sixpence I could have eaten six. This won't give either of us enough. But something is better than nothing."
She told the little beggar, "Wait here a moment."
Inside, the shop was warm and full of delicious smells. The woman was about to add another batch of hot buns to the window display.
Sara held out her poor little coin. "Please, have you lost a silver fourpence?" she asked. "A fourpenny piece like this?"
The woman examined the coin, then the child: the earnest little face and the bedraggled clothes that had once been fine.
"Goodness, no," she replied. "Was it you who found it?"
"Yes, down in the gutter," Sara answered.
"Then it's yours to keep," the woman said. "It might have lain there a week. Heaven knows whose it was—you certainly can't find out."
"I realize that," replied Sara, "but I thought I ought to ask you first."
Puzzlement, interest, and kindness mingled in the woman's face. "There aren't many who'd ask," she said.
Noticing Sara's eyes turn towards the buns, she added, "Would you like to buy something?"
"Please may I have four buns," Sara said, "the ones that cost a penny each?"
At the window, the woman began filling a paper bag with buns.
Sara counted six going into the bag.
"I only asked for four, please," she pointed out. "Fourpence is all I have."
The woman gave her kindly look. "The extra two are makeweight—I'll throw them in. You'll find time to eat them, I expect. Aren't you hungry?"
Sara's eyes filled with a mist.

"Yes, very hungry," she replied. "I'm most grateful for your kindness, and—" She had meant to explain that a child outside was even hungrier than she was. At that moment, however, two or three customers entered together, each apparently in a great hurry. All Sara could do was thank the woman once more and leave.

The beggar girl remained curled up at the corner of the step. Her filthy, wet rags made her look dreadful. She stared blankly ahead, her expression dulled by suffering. Suddenly Sara saw her drag the back of a rough, blackened hand across her eyes. Tears had forced themselves beneath her lids, apparently surprising her, and she was wiping them away. She muttered under her breath.
Opening the paper bag, Sara pulled out a hot bun. Already its warmth had begun to take the chill from her own hands.
She placed it in the girl's rag-covered lap. "Look, it's lovely and hot," she said. "Eat it; it'll help with the hunger."
The girl gave a start and stared up at her, almost frightened by this astonishing turn of luck. Then she seized the bun and stuffed it into her mouth in enormous, wolf-like bites.
In hoarse, frantic delight she cried, "Oh, my! Oh, my! OH my!" Sara could hear it clearly.
From the bag Sara drew three further buns and set them down.
Something terrible sounded in that hoarse voice, so ravenously hungry.
"Her hunger is worse than mine," Sara told herself. "She's starving." Her hand shook as she laid down the fourth bun. Then she said, "I'm not starving," and added the fifth.

As Sara turned away, the little savage of London went on snatching and devouring. Her ravenous hunger left no room for thanks, even had anyone taught her manners, which nobody had. She was simply a poor little wild creature.
Sara said, "Good-bye."

From across the road she glanced back. With a bun in each hand, the child had paused halfway through a mouthful to watch her. Sara nodded gently. After another long, curious stare, the girl jerked her tangled head in reply. Until Sara disappeared, she took no further bite and did not even finish the mouthful already begun.
Just then, the woman in the bakery glanced through her window.
"Well, I never!" she exclaimed. "She's handed those buns to a beggar child! And it wasn't for lack of wanting them herself. Dear me, she looked hungry enough. I'd like to know what made her do that."
For a few moments she remained behind the glass, thinking. Curiosity finally won. She went to the doorway to question the child on the step.
"Who gave you your buns?" she asked. The child pointed with her head towards Sara, now disappearing in the distance.
The woman asked, "What did she tell you?"
The rough voice replied, "Wanted to know if I was hungry."
"And what was your answer?"
"Told her I was."
"So she went into the shop, bought the buns, and brought them out for you?"
The girl nodded back.
"How many buns?"
"Five."
The woman stood considering that.
Quietly she said, "Only one left for herself, then. She could have eaten all six, too. I could tell by looking at her eyes."
She watched the bedraggled little figure far down the street. Her usually comfortable mind felt more unsettled than it had for a long time.
"I wish she hadn't hurried off," she said. "Bless me, I'd have given her a dozen." Then she turned back to the girl.
"Do you still feel hungry?" she asked.
"Always hungry, me," the girl replied. "Only it's not quite so bad now."
Holding the shop door wide, the woman said, "Come inside with me."
The child rose and shuffled through. An invitation into warmth, into a place full of bread, seemed impossible to believe. She had no idea what would happen next. She hardly cared.

Pointing towards the fire in the small back room, the woman said, "Warm yourself there. And listen: whenever you're desperate for some bread, come here and ask. For that little girl's sake, bless me if I won't give you some."
The bun she had kept gave Sara a little comfort. At least it was still very hot, and better than an empty stomach. As she walked she tore off tiny pieces, eating slowly so they would last.
"Imagine it's a magic bun," she said, "with every bite equal to a whole dinner. If I carried on eating at this rate, I'd be having far too much."

By the time she came to the square containing the Select Seminary, darkness had fallen and all the houses were lit. The blinds were still open in the room where she so often saw the Large Family. At this hour she frequently found the man she called Mr. Montmorency in a big chair, surrounded by a swarm of children. They talked and laughed, perched on his knees or the chair's arms, or leaned against him. Tonight they swarmed around him as usual, but he was standing. A considerable bustle was underway. Someone was evidently leaving on a journey, and that someone was Mr. Montmorency. Outside waited a brougham with a large portmanteau strapped to it. The children danced, chattered, and clung to their father. Their pretty, rosy mother stood close by, talking as if settling last-minute questions. Sara stopped briefly to watch the smaller children lifted for kisses, and their father bend to kiss the older ones too.
"Will he be gone for long, I wonder?" she thought. "That's quite a large portmanteau. Oh dear, they'll miss him so much! I'll miss him too, though he doesn't even know I exist."
Remembering the sixpence, she moved on when the front door opened. But she saw the traveller emerge against the warm light of the hall, with the older children still clustered close.
Janet, the little girl, asked, "Will there be snow all over Moscow? And ice everywhere?"
Another called, "Will you ride in a drosky? Are you going to see the Czar?"

Laughing, he promised, "I'll tell you everything in my letters. And I'll send pictures of muzhiks and other things. Inside with you now. It's a horrible wet night. I'd far rather stay here with you than set off for Moscow. Good night! Good night, my duckies! God bless you!" He hurried down the steps and sprang into the brougham.
Bouncing on the doormat, Guy Clarence shouted, "When you find the little girl, tell her we send our love."
Then the children went inside and closed the door.

On their way back to the room, Janet asked Nora, "Did you notice the little-girl-who-is-not-a-beggar going past? She looked cold and soaked, and I saw her glance back over her shoulder at us. Mamma says her clothes always seem to have been given away by someone very rich, someone who parted with them only because they'd grown too shabby to wear. That school sends her on errands on the very worst days and nights."
Feeling faint and unsteady, Sara crossed to the area steps leading down to Miss Minchin's basement.
She wondered, "Who is that little girl—the one he's setting out to find?"

Dragging her basket, which now felt terribly heavy indeed, she went down the area steps. Meanwhile the Large Family's father drove swiftly towards the station to catch the train that would carry him to Moscow, where he would do everything he could to trace Captain Crewe's lost little daughter.
